articles.title: Who Cut In On Your Race?
articles.dek: Paul asks the Galatians a question borrowed from the racetrack — then answers it with a word borrowed from the battlefield.
articles.quote: Freedom was never permission to run alone — it was an invitation to keep in step, all the way to the line.
articles.body:
Barcelona, August 1992. Derek Redmond steps into the blocks for the 400-meter semifinal, the race of his life. The gun cracks. He explodes off the line, and 150 meters in, he is running the best time of his career — until his hamstring snaps. He crumples on the track, face twisted, and waves the medics away. Then, slowly, impossibly, he stands up and starts hopping toward the finish line on one leg, because something in him refuses to be carried off that track.

That is when a man in a blue shirt and a white cap vaults over the railing, shoves past a security guard, and runs onto the track. It is Jim Redmond, Derek's father. He wraps his arm around his son's waist and says, so the cameras barely catch it, “You don't have to do this.” Derek says he does. So together, son leaning on father, they walk the last 120 meters while 65,000 people stand and roar. Derek Redmond does not win a medal that day. He finishes anyway, arm in arm with the one person who refused to let him finish alone.

Paul, writing to a group of young churches in Galatia, reaches for the same picture. These believers had started so well — they had heard the gospel of grace, believed it, and begun running. Then teachers arrived insisting they needed something extra: circumcision, law-keeping, a religious performance added on top of grace. Paul does not open with a lecture. He opens with a question, and it still stings.

“You were running a good race. Who cut in on you and kept you from obeying the truth?” (Gal 5:7, NIV)

Here is something worth noticing: the phrase “cut in on you” is not a vague metaphor. In Paul's world it was athletic slang for a runner who elbows another off the track, or veers into someone's lane to break their stride. But the same word was also used for armies tearing up a road to stop advancing troops — sabotaging the route itself. Paul's readers, most of them Gentiles who knew both the stadium and the highway, would have felt it instantly. Someone had deliberately broken up the road these believers were running on. Paul names the danger with a small, homely image next: “A little yeast works through the whole batch of dough” (Gal 5:9). It doesn't take a landslide to derail a race. A pebble in the shoe is enough, if you run on it long enough.

What follows in the chapter reads like commentary on a race gone wrong. Paul warns that freedom is not a finish line you cross alone: “You, my brothers and sisters, were called to be free. But do not use your freedom to indulge the flesh; rather, serve one another humbly in love” (Gal 5:13). Then comes a warning that sounds almost animal: “If you bite and devour each other, watch out that you are not destroyed by each other” (Gal 5:15). Picture injured runners, tangled together, snapping at each other mid-race instead of helping each other up. That is what envy, rivalry, and self-righteousness do to a community. They turn teammates into obstacles.

Against that, Paul lists what a life led by the Spirit actually produces — not effort, but fruit: “love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control” (Gal 5:22–23). This is what someone still on the road looks like. Not flawless. Not fast. Just recognizably headed the right direction, bearing the marks of Someone else's life growing in them.

And then Paul closes the whole section with a second racing image, and this is the detail that changes how I read the passage. “Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit” (Gal 5:25). “Keep in step” translates a Greek military word for marching in formation, rank by rank, matching your stride to the soldier beside you. Paul opened this chapter with someone tearing up the road to break your stride. He closes it with an invitation to match your stride to the Spirit's instead. The chapter is bookended by two pictures of the same race — one person trying to wreck it, and Another offering to run it with you.

That is exactly what happened on that track in Barcelona. An injury tried to end Derek Redmond's race. It could not, because his father refused to let him finish it alone. The medal was never the point that day, and I don't think Paul thinks winning is the point either. Obeying the truth, staying free, loving your neighbor — none of it depends on running faster than everyone else. It depends on who you let keep step with you when your hamstring gives out.

So ask honestly: what has cut in on your race lately? Maybe it's comparison — measuring your walk with God against someone else's stride. Maybe it's a smaller, more respectable kind of legalism, the quiet belief that grace got you started but effort has to finish the job. Maybe it's simply exhaustion, the sense that you're hopping toward a line you're not sure you'll reach. Paul's answer isn't try harder. It's keep in step — let the Spirit set the pace, and let him carry what you cannot.

You don't have to finish this one alone. Someone already vaulted the railing for you. Take the next step in step with him, and let that be enough for today.

articles.title: The Ember Under the Ash
articles.dek: Long before matches, Filipino households kept fire alive overnight by banking embers in ash — a quiet skill that turns out to be exactly how God treats the barely-burning.
articles.quote: Real strength isn't measured by how loud it can shout — it's measured by how gently it can hold what's already broken.
articles.illustration: banking embers in a probinsya kalan
articles.body:
Before there were matches in most Philippine homes, there was ash. Every night, before the household slept, someone — usually a lola, usually without being asked twice — would rake the coals of the kalan into a small mound and bury them under a blanket of cold ash. Not to put the fire out. To keep it alive. Ash traps heat the way a blanket traps warmth. By morning, when she uncovered that mound, she wouldn't find flame. She would find something smaller and far more fragile: a dull orange glow, barely holding on, easy to miss if you weren't looking for it. She would kneel down, cup her hands around it, and blow. Not hard — hard would scatter the ash and choke what little heat remained. Just steady, patient breath, until the glow caught a curl of dry coconut husk, and the curl caught a twig, and the twig became the fire that cooked the rice for a whole family's day.

It is a small, ordinary skill, nearly forgotten now that a lighter costs less than a jeepney fare. But it is worth remembering, because it is almost exactly the picture God paints of himself in Isaiah 42 — and the contrast with the chapter just before it is what makes it sing.

Isaiah 41 is a courtroom scene. God is calling the nations to bring their strongest case, their strongest gods, and see whose word actually holds up under pressure. And what we find, almost comically, is that the gods of the nations need help standing. Isaiah describes craftsmen huddled over their idols, encouraging each other: "The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer spurs on him who strikes the anvil... 'It is good,' he says; he nails down the idol so it will not topple" (Isaiah 41:7). Read that again. Their god needs to be nailed to the floor so it doesn't fall over. That is the honest picture of manufactured strength — loud, polished, and one nudge from collapse.

Then, right at the start of chapter 42, God introduces someone entirely different. Not a idol needing to be propped up, but a servant who needs no propping at all: "Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen one in whom I delight; I will put my Spirit on him, and he will bring justice to the nations. He will not shout or cry out, or raise his voice in the streets" (Isaiah 42:1–2). No hammering. No nailing down. No need to be louder than the competition. And then comes the line that turns the whole picture upside down.

A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not snuff out; in faithfulness he will bring forth justice. (Isaiah 42:3)

Picture what a bruised reed is actually good for. Nothing, practically. A reed grows by a riverbank, hollow and thin, and once it's bent or cracked, it can't hold weight, can't be woven, can't do what a reed is supposed to do. The efficient thing — the thing any of us would do without thinking twice — is to snap it the rest of the way and toss it aside. And a smoldering wick is even less impressive. It isn't burning. It's barely glowing, giving off more smoke than light, one draft of wind away from going cold and useless. The efficient thing is to pinch it out and replace it with a fresh one.

What Isaiah is describing, centuries before Jesus ever walked into a synagogue, is a coming King whose greatness will be proven by the opposite instinct. He will not finish off what's already failing. He will not discard what's already struggling. Matthew later quotes this exact passage to describe how Jesus moved through crowds of the sick and the broken — not shouting, not showing off, but healing quietly, one bruised person at a time (Matthew 12:15–21). The measure of his power was never how many people he could overpower. It was how gently he could handle the ones everyone else had already given up on.

Here's what's easy to miss on a first read: the reed doesn't get snapped, and the wick doesn't get snuffed — but neither one gets left exactly as it was, either. Isaiah says the servant does this "in faithfulness," on his way to establishing justice. This isn't a King who lowers his standards for the fragile. It's a King who understands that the fragile aren't finished — they're being tended toward something. The lola blowing on the embers isn't lowering her standards for dinner. She's patient with the ember precisely because she knows what it can still become.

Think about who in your life is a bruised reed right now. Maybe it's someone whose faith is down to embers — still going through the motions of Sunday, but privately unsure if any of it still holds weight. Maybe it's a coworker whose confidence got broken by one bad year, one harsh boss, one failure they can't stop replaying. Maybe, some mornings, it's you. The temptation, when we meet something bruised, is always efficiency: snap it off, move on, stop wasting time on what isn't producing. But that has never been how God treats what's struggling to stay lit. And it was never meant to be how we treat each other, either.

You don't have to be the one who reignites someone. You just have to be willing to cup your hands and breathe, gently, without demanding the flame come back on your schedule. That is a skill, not a talent — which means it can be practiced. The next time you're tempted to write someone off because they're dim, bent, barely holding on, remember the lola at dawn. She didn't see ash. She knelt down low enough to find the glow that was still there, and she gave it her breath until it became a fire that fed a family.

Someone near you is smoldering today, not dead. Kneel down. Breathe gently. Don't be in a hurry to see the flame — just be faithful to keep breathing on the ember until it is.

articles.title: The Waiting That Made Him Ready
articles.dek: Joseph's wisdom wasn't waiting in a cell to be released one day — it was being formed there. What if your delay is doing the same thing?
articles.quote: The years that tested Joseph were the same years that trained him — the waiting itself was the workshop where his wisdom was made.
articles.body:
On Robben Island, in a narrow strip of dirt between the prison wall and the yard, Nelson Mandela grew tomatoes, chilies, and onions. He asked for permission for years before he got it. When it finally came, he treated that patch of soil like it mattered more than anything else he owned — because in a place built to strip a man of everything, a garden was one of the only things left that he could still shape with his own hands. He learned the soil, timed the rains, shared his harvest with the same guards who had locked him in. And for a season, when he was secretly writing the story of his life at night, pages of that manuscript were hidden in tins buried among the vegetable beds, safer there than anywhere else on the island.

It's tempting to read that garden as a small mercy — something to pass the time. But look closer and it reads like something else entirely. A man who would one day need to lead a fractured nation without revenge in his hands was, decades earlier, practicing patience over a single row of tomatoes. Nobody watching him kneel in that dirt thought they were watching training. They thought they were watching a prisoner with a hobby.

Psalm 105 tells a story that runs on the same hidden track. It's a poem remembering how God kept his promises to Israel's ancestors, and right in the middle of it sits a compressed, breathless retelling of Joseph. "He sent a man before them — Joseph, sold as a slave," the psalm says (Ps 105:17). Sold by his own brothers. Shipped to Egypt. Then this: "They bruised his feet with shackles, his neck was put in irons" (Ps 105:18). Not a metaphor. An actual young man, falsely accused, actually chained, actually forgotten in an actual prison for years, while the dreams God had given him as a boy sat untouched and unproven.

Then comes the hinge of the whole passage:

till what he foretold came to pass, till the word of the LORD proved him true. (Ps 105:19, NIV)

Read that verse slowly and something surprising surfaces. It doesn't say Joseph waited until Pharaoh noticed him, or until his luck turned, or until someone finally believed his story. It says he waited until the word of the Lord proved him true — until the thing God had spoken over him was tested, refined, and shown to be solid. The Hebrew picture behind that phrase is close to what happens when metal is put through fire to burn off what doesn't belong. That's what the prison years were doing to Joseph. Not punishing him. Purifying him.

And notice what happens the very next moment in the psalm. No transition, no explanation — straight from irons to authority: "The king sent and released him... he made him lord of his house, ruler over all he possessed, to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom" (Ps 105:20–22). Where did that wisdom come from? The psalm doesn't say Joseph learned it in Pharaoh's palace, after the chains came off. It's placed right after the shackles, as if the wisdom he taught Egypt's elders was quietly assembled during the very years nobody was watching — in a cell, doing small things faithfully, with no evidence yet that any of it would matter.

That's the part most of us skip past when we tell Joseph's story. We rush from the pit to the palace, from disaster to promotion, because that's the satisfying part. But the psalm lingers on the years between — bruised feet, iron collar, unanswered dreams — and calls that stretch necessary. Not wasted. Not a delay before the real story starts. It was the real story, just not the part anyone could see yet.

Mandela wouldn't have called himself a Joseph. But the shape is the same. Twenty-seven years is a long time to be tested, and what came out the other side of it wasn't just a free man — it was a man who could sit across from the people who had jailed him and choose a truth commission over a firing squad. That kind of restraint isn't manufactured on the day of release. It's grown, slowly, in ordinary years, over ordinary things. A garden. A patient word to a guard. A decision, made over and over in the dark, not to let bitterness win the argument it was constantly making.

Here's where this lands for you and me, because most of us aren't waiting on a prison release — we're waiting on something quieter. A marriage that hasn't healed yet. A diagnosis with no clear timeline. A job search that keeps circling without landing. A gift you know God gave you that nobody else has noticed yet. It's easy to treat that waiting room as empty time — as if life is on pause until the door opens. Psalm 105 suggests something gentler and more hopeful: the door hasn't opened yet because the person walking through it isn't finished being made ready. The very patience the waiting is costing you may be the exact thing you'll need to carry once it ends.

So do the small, unglamorous thing in front of you today — the tomato row, the kind word, the honest work nobody applauds. Not because it will hurry the outcome along, but because it's shaping the hands that will one day hold what you've been waiting for. God rarely explains the wait while you're in it. But he is never wasting it.

articles.title: The Jersey Mandela Chose to Wear
articles.dek: Why the gentlest possible answer once undid decades of wrath in a single stadium, and what it says about the thirty seconds before you reply.
articles.quote: A gentle answer isn't weakness performing peace, it's strength choosing it.
articles.body:
On June 24, 1995, Nelson Mandela walked out onto the field at Ellis Park Stadium in Johannesburg wearing a green and gold jersey. Not a suit. Not a dashiki. A rugby jersey — the exact one worn by the Springboks, South Africa's national team, and for most of the twentieth century a symbol white South Africans loved and black South Africans loathed. Under apartheid, the Springbok emblem had stood for the government that jailed Mandela for twenty-seven years. Many of his own supporters had wanted the team's name and colors abolished entirely.

Instead, Mandela put it on. Number six, matching team captain Francois Pienaar. He walked into a stadium of sixty-two thousand people, the vast majority white Afrikaners, many of whom had cheered the system that once locked him away. He had every reason, and every right, to greet them with a speech about what they had cost him. He had spent nearly three decades with nothing to do but rehearse that speech, if he wanted to.

He said nothing of the kind. He simply stood there in their colors. And the crowd — stunned, then thunderous — began to chant his name. "Nelson! Nelson!" A stadium that had every reason to expect his wrath instead received his welcome. South Africa went on to win the World Cup that night, and when a reporter asked captain Francois Pienaar what it felt like to have sixty-two thousand fans behind him, he gave an answer almost as famous as Mandela's gesture: "We didn't have sixty-two thousand fans behind us today. We had forty-three million South Africans." Historians still point to that afternoon as one of the moments that helped a fractured nation believe reconciliation was possible, not just as policy, but as something a person could actually choose to do with his body, in public, at cost to his own dignity.

Mandela did not invent that principle. A king wrote it down roughly three thousand years earlier, in a single proverb so short it is easy to read past it.

"A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger." (Proverbs 15:1, NIV)

Solomon follows that opening line with three more, each one turning the same jewel to catch a different bit of light. "The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge, but the mouth of the fool gushes folly" (v.2). "The eyes of the LORD are everywhere, keeping watch on the wicked and the good" (v.3) — a reminder, right in the middle of a passage about speech, that we are never talking in private. And then the line that quietly stops you: "The soothing tongue is a tree of life, but a perverse tongue crushes the spirit" (v.4).

Here is what's easy to miss on a fast read: Solomon isn't describing two personality types, the naturally calm person and the naturally hotheaded one. He's describing two answers, sitting side by side, both available to the very same person in the very same moment. The Hebrew word behind "gentle" is rak — tender, soft, pliable. It's the same word used elsewhere for young grass and for the vulnerability of a child. It is not a synonym for weak. It describes something that could have been hard, and chose not to be.

That's the turn worth sitting with. Mandela's gentleness at Ellis Park wasn't the absence of strength — it took more strength than the speech he could have given. A harsh word is often the easy word, the reflex word, the one that requires no restraint at all. A gentle answer is the harder one to build, because you have to hold your own wound still long enough to choose it.

Notice, too, what verse 4 promises the gentle tongue: it becomes "a tree of life." That phrase appears only a handful of times in the whole Old Testament, and every other time it shows up, it's describing something planted in Eden, something that gives life simply by being near it (Genesis 2:9; 3:22). Solomon is saying your words can do that. A soft answer in a tense room doesn't just avoid a fight — it plants something that keeps growing after the conversation ends. And the reverse is just as real: a perverse or reckless tongue, he says, "crushes the spirit." Not just hurts feelings. Crushes something in a person that may take a long time to stand back up.

This is where the gospel meets the proverb, because Jesus is the only person who ever lived this out perfectly, under far worse provocation than any of us will face. Peter writes that "when they hurled their insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he entrusted himself to him who judges justly" (1 Peter 2:23). At the cross, wrath — real wrath, God's own just anger at everything broken in us — met the gentlest possible answer: not silence, not a shrug, but a Savior absorbing it so it would turn away from us for good (Romans 5:8–9). Every gentle answer we manage to give another person is a small echo of the one Jesus gave for us at infinite cost.

A gentle answer isn't weakness performing peace — it's strength choosing it. That's worth carrying into your next hard conversation, whether it's a message from a coworker that stung, a sibling who said the wrong thing at dinner, or a comment thread you're tempted to answer at 11 p.m.

Think of the family group chat that goes quiet and tense after somebody's comment lands wrong. The tita who corrects you in front of everyone at the reunion. The office chat where a boss's one-line message reads harsher than they probably meant it. Every one of those is a small Ellis Park moment — a chance to hand back either a stadium's worth of wrath or a stadium's worth of welcome. Solomon isn't asking you to pretend the sting isn't real. He's asking what you'll do with it in the next thirty seconds, because that's usually all the time you actually have before the reply gets typed and sent.

You won't feel like Mandela walking into Ellis Park. You'll feel like someone with a perfectly good, perfectly deserved harsh word loaded and ready. That's exactly the moment Proverbs 15:1 is written for. Not for the easy days, but for the one text message, the one meeting, the one family gathering where you get to decide which tongue you'll bring: one that crushes, or one that's a tree of life to somebody who badly needs it.

Before you answer today, pause half a breath longer than feels natural. Ask what a gentle word would cost you right now — and whether it might be worth planting anyway.
